sections.title: Chairman's Chat
sections.content:
Tam (AKA Glorious Leader) reports

Crickey, a year doesn’t last long nowadays - must be something to do with age I guess. Around this time last year I decided that I would put Martin out of his misery and volunteer to be Chair when he stood down, seeing as no one else had stuck their hand up. And now here we are, on the verge of the winter club nights starting, AGM notice in this edition of Skywords and the Farmers’ Dinner less than a month away - all signs that the season is drawing to a close. For many, a stunning season, well done all - the club as a whole in pole position in the XCLeague, surely they can’t be caught now, 3 of our Sky Gods in the national top 10, many pilots achieving their best year ever and due to receive a new club mug (see Chris Fountains report in this mag) and new CPs coming through and getting good flights. Rich Meek, currently on an acro course looks to just miss out on topping the individual XC league for the second year after his 2 successive wins in previous years. Truly, a great time to be in the club, and long may it last. I can highly recommend both attending the club night to hear Ed Cleasby speak, and the Farmers’ Dinner.  For the newbies, Ed is a bona fide legend and oracle in our sport who continues to give his time to help develop other people’s flying - well worth a drive to listen to. The Farmers’ Dinner (Oct 17th) is where we invite “our farmers” to a slap up meal at the  Knight’s Table, Stainforth near Settle, to thank them for the use of their land for the year - more details are available here.

From a personal point of view, retirement wasn’t meant to be like this! I may not be able to fly but I’m getting pretty good at wielding a paint brush. Next year is clearly going to be my time, watch out all!  See you on a hill , or at the above events, soon!

Whernside to Sunderland, September 28th

Chris Kay reports

Whitburn

The gaggle of six that left Whernside disintegrated over Widdale. Alan Oliver and I managed to stay together the longest. We got as far as Bainbridge, where I last saw him turning circles over the Roman fort. Alan headed along Wensleydale to Leyburn whilst I went northeast, crossing Swaledale and Arkengarthdale at height until I was looking down upon the A66. I thought about landing for an easier retrieve but decided to push on. A bit of crosswinding around blue holes and a couple of fairly desperate low saves (I was desperate not to land near Bishop Auckland again) got me within sight of Durham where I really was going to call it a day. I’d picked out a landing field and was taking photos of the cathedral when my vario started beeping. It was getting late, but the sky beyond looked good, and so I carried on, eventually making it to Sunderland, quite a sight with the now low sun casting long shadows and glinting off the river. After a short, not at all sketchy trip out to sea, I landed just up the coast, an hour before sunset, near an old red and white striped lighthouse.

Some pics here

sections.title: Coaching
sections.content:
Pete Logan, Chief Coach reports

 

Looking up to Hawkswick Wood & Moor from Skirfare’s bend.  

I love it when a plan comes together. The Dales’ best hill for beginners, Windbank, delivered fantastic late season conditions yesterday (28th Sept) and Jordan from Active Edge delivered five new club pilots itching for some airtime. The airmass and forecasts came good with a promised five star set of conditions from late morning to late afternoon.

The walk up was in nil wind and there were some disconcerting wafts of wind from the SSE on take off as we got some site briefing out of the way. After just a little parawaiting, Jordan was needing to get back down to drive over and meet his students at Tow Scar, but what we thought was going to be a sled ride down turned into a bit of soaring on Knipe. I was encouraged by this and went along onto Hawkswick Moor to float gently up in gentle ridge and thermic lift.

The late sun just takes time to mix the upper wind properly and bring it onto the hill. Pretty much after that it was easy to reverse launch and, at times, strong wind launch and top land on TO. In the air the thermals were pretty gentle at 1 to 1.5m/s and working well out in front too which meant no one was in each other’s way pinned on the ridge. New CPs could also get a fair way down the ridge without having to worry about not getting back to the bottom landing. There were some 3m/s bullets but they’re narrow at this time of year and never last too long. Climbs to 600 and 700m were regular. You couldn’t wish for better conditions for new pilots getting to grips with thermal flying without the immediate panic of going down if you lost the thermal.

For those club pilots who’ve crossed off their Pilot Rating tasks this year, Clive, the other coaches and myself will be happy to help with study for the Pilot Rating exam. Do get in touch on the Telegram group: https://t.me/+bnohZh-j7s84N2Q8  or at coaching@dhpc.org.uk

sections.title: DHPC AGM
sections.content:
Clive Sury DHPC Sec reports

DHPC Annual General Meeting

Thursday December 3rd 2026. 7.30 for 8 pm start

Horse and Farrier, Bridge St, Otley. LS21 1BQ

All members of the Dales Hang Gliding and Paragliding Club are invited to attend the AGM, which will be followed by the presentation of the coveted club trophies and mugs for the 2026 season.

All proposals will be published in the November edition of Skywords and on the club forum. The Treasurer's report and reports from the other current committee members will be published on the forum by November 17th (members only). There will be no opportunity to raise new issues for voting after 1st November, or on the night at the AGM. Voting on all proposals will be at the AGM in person only.

As well as setting membership subscriptions and contributions to the Flying Fund for the coming year, all committee posts are up for re-election, as per the constitution. Members are free to stand for any post - none of the current incumbents will be offended if you wish to have a go at their role. Committee membership simply requires a little spare time and a willingness to put something back into the club. If you want to have a non-committal conversation about a role, then please contact the Chairman, Tam Morrison, at chairman@dhpc.org.uk, or Secretary Clive Sury at secretary@dhpc.org.uk

sections.title: Safety
sections.content:
Rob Urselmann reports

If you’re anything into XC, the “2026 Mugs” article above might be almost FOMO inducing. How much do we push ourselves for those coveted mugs or competition points?
The art of balancing performance and safety is a fine line.

So far, in my four years of flying after qualifying in August ‘22, I received four mugs (50,100,200,300km). The first one after merely 2.5 months flying as I blissfully unaware was recording my ridge flights in XCLeague for my own record, and a mere two beats up & down the likes of Whernside, Ingleborough or Windbank can net you 20km without even leaving the ridge. Unofficially, and without the current hard stop to XC flying as CP, I had already logged a few XC flights in France, including the Petit Tour de Annecy in my first 20 hours. That, and no doubt being surrounded by the XC gods in J36, put XC foremost in my mind. I scrambled and sat my Pilot exam early in my second season in order to partake in the BPCup (only for that to be canned last minute due to abysmal weather), but I was now ready for my first ‘proper’ XC season (and 100km mug at the end).

Having flown through one very cold winter in my open harness, in May ‘23 I purchased a used pod. Now this happened to come as a really good wing-pod deal with only 2 hours on the wing. Since I had only 45 hours airtime on the clock, my intention was to immediately flog the wing on. Now, being fairly light (mid range, sometimes below) on my low-B and regularly flying in top-end conditions, I had seen my fair number of flying and landing vertical or even going backward. So, with benign conditions forecast, I decided to have one little test flight on this high-B before switching to the pod.  Not having ground handled it yet before walking up, I laid the wing out, inspected it and pulled up in lightish wind for a good session of ground handling first. However the wing had other ideas and I was airborne in a second. So much for GH before first flight on a new wing. Whoops.  But the flight was lovely; the Chili 5 was just soo much more responsive than my ‘old’ Geo 6, telling me what the air was doing instead of wafting around above my head with (to me) little feedback. I fell in love and ended up flying the Chili for 10 hours before switching harnesses and selling my complete ‘out-of-school’ setup instead. In hindsight this was possibly a bit early.

I flew my first ‘big’ XC a few months later. After bombing out on top of Barkin coming from Gragareth, I relaunched late in the day at 5pm, got a solid thermal and flew the seabreeze convergence all the way to Grasmere, hitting 2100m on the way, landing there on the eve of the LCC.

Giving safety a nudge I booked an SIV in Annecy in September, after a few flights during family holiday in the Dolomites. During one of those I hit a leeside thermal and next instance I had the Chili, fully inflated, in vertical position at 90° next to me. Somehow I must have done the right thing (or more likely, just not the wrong thing!), recovered and flew on. Pure luck; my SIV was still a week away!

During the SIV I struggled with the spin appreciation, didn’t correct in time on recovery, ended up in a double twist in auto-rotation and tossing the laundry (reserve). As I was pulled into the rescue boat, my SIV buddy in sequence after me decided to do another drill on the way to the beach and lost too much height to make it back, so I was dumped and we were off to pull him out. My first flight the next day I took it easy to get rid of the nerves and spend the rest of that final day redrilling spins whilst the others were progressing to wing-overs etc. Despite that less-than-optimal experience, I left the SIV with a much better understanding of the wing’s character and its behaviour in turbulent air.

If you, like I was, get a bit nervous every time the wing ‘judders’ overhead due to turbulence (or a spicy thermal), I can definitely recommend an SIV.

The following season I had a great time and bagged my 200km mug … before crashing on Ingleborough mid October and doing some serious damage (covered in SkyWords Nov-25). However I was back flying within 4 months, as soon as the bones and muscles were healed, well in time for last years XC season. Despite taking it very gently to begin with, I managed my 300km mug, and came close to my 100km T-shirt (I just shouldn’t have stopped at Goal, where I arrived at base and spend 20mins getting down in very buoyant conditions)

As I’ve written here before, following a suspiciously high number of partial collapses and being aware I was flying pretty low in the weight range (85-87kg on this 75-95kg wing), toward the end of last season I started flying with some ballast. That instantly solved the problem, and I have had one tiny flutter and that was falling out of a spicey thermal. Now with the wing stable, probably also due to me flying with a bit more tension on the brakes (something very hard to coach it turns out, and potentially some long hangover from me pulling too hard during that SIV??), I was getting proper confident and dynamic again in the air.

Ever keen for more performance, I have been eying up the step-up to a C wing for a while. However, whilst I had issues flying the Chili, I always put that idea firmly back in the bag “until I can properly fly this wing”. But at the same time I figured I should try a few potential candidates to see how I felt on other high-B’s or low-C’s.  In January, whilst visiting S&W and them having it on demo, I talked myself into taking the new Ozone Delta 5 two-liner low-C home for testing. But as it sat here waiting for a flyable weather window, I found myself getting anxious about what would happen if it wasn’t benign weather for that test flight and how I would deal with any departure-from-normal-flight. In the end, one of the best flying decisions I think I ever made, I left it in the bag and handed it back. As one of my mates (you know who you are) put it aptly “I think you will find the delta a lot of fun to fly until it stops flying.”

I was, and still am, wary of two-liners. But I had my eyes set on testing the ‘new’ 2.5 liner Alpina GT (“for pilots who want the feel, handling and performance of the classic 3 line EN C glider but do not need the additional performance offered by a 2-line design“)

Then, eight months later and now fully in swing on the Chili (flying it dynamic and on half-full bar a lot of the time), an Alpina4 in my size up came for sale in August. Having a fair few hours on it (but still much less than the 233 I have on the Chili) it was, as they say, reasonably priced. So I made enquiries and being local(ish), I was allowed to take the wing and test fly it. This time, having learned from that first go on the Chili, I spent a few hours GH it in a big, clear, clean paddock in a stiff breeze, and liked what I saw and felt. I then took it up my local wee hill on a calm evening, and it was love at first flight so I bought it (really should’ve negotiated harder lol). I possibly should’ve waited for a more dynamic flight and see how I felt after that before committing, but those post-purchase worries would turn out unnecessary.  Despite a lot of non-flyable weather and me being away for a while, I’ve now got 11 flights and over 10 hours on it, some of which in fairly spicy conditions. I don’t know how much is from it being lighter weight, a 2.5 liner, low-C or a different brand design philosophy, but I get on really well with the Alpina: yes it’s more dynamic than the Chili but at the same time it ‘communicates’ better what it’s doing, so whilst more active I actually find it just a little less effort to fly and easier to thermal.

But my biggest safety vs performance gain this year has nothing to do with equipment. This year, whilst keeping an eye on that possible 100km T-shirt, my main focus was to improve my skills and just to enjoy myself. I ‘only’ managed 49 hours this calendar year (vs 70 each the two years before) and only two flights over 50km, but I have a good year balancing first-most fun, working on skills on non-XC days, and making the most of performance during good XC days. Whilst there may have been a few in-flight moments that could’ve been better, I’ve always landed with a big grin this year, happy with the flight and the balance between performance and safety.

IMHO the best metric for anybody's personal flying is always the size of the grin on your face after you’ve landed; no matter what your goals are (comp, skills, making Goal, first thermal to base, or just a leisurely evening boat-about), if you’ve achieved what you set out to do that grin will be there.


Happy flying. Fly safe, fly far, big grins.
